abstract: Florivory is an important biotic challenge in plant-insect interactions, evoking induced responses in plant specialised metabolism, the extent of which depends on phenotypic plasticity. While responses to leaf herbivores are well studied, floral responses to florivores with different feeding modes, their systemic effects on leaves and the role of intraspecific chemodiversity remain poorly understood. We used clonal replicates of five Tanacetum vulgare (Asteraceae) chemotypes, which differ in their leaf and flower terpene profiles, to test how florivory by chewing beetles (Olibrus spp.) and phloem-feeding aphids (Macrosiphoniella tanacetaria) affects the metabolic responses of flower heads and systemically in leaves. Floral volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and stored terpenes were analysed via GC-MS and metabolic fingerprints via LC-MS. While overall metabolic profiles of flower heads and leaves remained largely stable following florivory, specific metabolites shifted in abundance locally and systemically. These changes primarily involved the shikimate and phenylpropanoid pathways and minor terpenes. The specific metabolic responses varied by florivore species and chemotype, a pattern observed across floral VOCs, as well as stored terpenes and untargeted metabolic fingerprints, differing also between organs. Overall, florivory triggers organ-specific chemical responses in reproductive and vegetative tissues, shaped by a complex interplay between plant chemotype and florivore type.
